title: Triangles
coreInsight: Triangle side and angle constraints are linked, and special triangles gain additional consequences from equality and symmetry.
targetLearnerRealization: A triangle's angles always total 180°, equal sides face equal angles regardless of orientation, and exterior angles follow from those same constraints.
learningObjectives: Use the 180° triangle angle sum in a specifically identified triangle.
Infer equal opposite angles from equal sides and equal opposite sides from equal angles.
Classify triangles by stated properties rather than orientation.
Derive an exterior angle through triangle sum and a straight-line supplement.
Enumerate all possible angle roles in an isosceles triangle without overlap.

continuity.openingCallback: Use a straight 180° angle as the fixed total into which a triangle's three corner turns can be rearranged.
closingSeeds: A right triangle adds one fixed 90° angle to the triangle constraints.
Triangles can be used as pieces for understanding polygon angle sums.

misconceptionTargets.misconception: A rotated or unfamiliar shape stops being isosceles.
Equal sides and equal opposite angles are unrelated facts.
Triangle angle sum can be used without identifying the relevant triangle.
Exterior and interior angles are interchangeable.

beats.purpose: Turn G1's moving-triangle question into a test of an invariant total.
beats.expectedRealization: Individual angles can change as a vertex moves, but their sum remains 180°.
beats.transitionIn: A straight angle totals 180°. Imagine detaching a triangle's three corner wedges and placing them side by side.
beats.whyNow: The changing-shape contrast creates the need for a stable triangle relationship.
beats.entryBridge: Compare the three-angle total before and after moving one vertex.
beats.exitBridge: The angles redistribute, but together still fill one straight angle.
learnerPrompts: Which quantity stays fixed when the vertex moves without collapsing the triangle?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. The three angles still total 180° even though their individual measures change.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Picture all three corner wedges placed together along a straight line.

visual.ariaLabel: Two differently shaped triangles whose three angle measures each sum to one hundred eighty degrees

steps.title: Rearrange the corners
steps.body: The three interior angle wedges exactly fill a straight angle, so their measures total 180°.

steps.title: Separate change from invariance
steps.body: Moving a vertex changes the shares of 180°, not the total.

resolution.takeaway: Every nondegenerate triangle has interior angle sum 180°.

beats.purpose: Connect equal sides with their opposite equal angles.
beats.expectedRealization: In an isosceles triangle, equal sides face equal angles.
beats.transitionIn: The 180° total constrains all triangles. Equal side lengths add another constraint.
beats.prompt: Triangle PQR has PQ = PR and angle Q = 58°. What is angle R?
beats.correctFeedback: Yes. Equal sides PQ and PR face equal angles R and Q.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Mark which angle lies opposite each of the equal sides.

steps.title: Match opposite parts
steps.body: Side PQ lies opposite angle R; side PR lies opposite angle Q. Since the sides match, those angles match.

steps.title: Check the triangle
steps.body: The vertex angle is 180° − 58° − 58° = 64°, confirming all three angles are positive and sum to 180°.

resolution.takeaway: Equal sides face equal angles—and equal angles face equal sides.

beats.purpose: Make classification depend on defining properties rather than orientation.
beats.expectedRealization: Rotation changes neither side equality nor triangle type.
beats.transitionIn: Keep the equal-side marks attached and rotate the entire figure.
beats.prompt: A triangle is turned so its point faces left. Two sides are still marked equal. Which classification is guaranteed?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. Isosceles means at least two equal sides; direction is irrelevant.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Use the tick marks, not where the point faces.

steps.title: Read properties
steps.body: The two equal lengths remain equal under rotation, so the defining isosceles property remains true.

resolution.takeaway: A triangle's type comes from its relationships, not its pose.

beats.purpose: Derive the exterior-angle relationship rather than present it as disconnected vocabulary.
beats.expectedRealization: An exterior angle supplements its adjacent interior angle and equals the sum of the two remote interior angles.
beats.transitionIn: Extend one triangle side. The new exterior angle and the nearby interior angle now fill a straight line.
beats.prompt: A triangle has remote interior angles 46° and 71°. What is the exterior angle at the third vertex?
beats.incorrectFeedback: First find the third interior angle, then take its supplement.

steps.title: Complete the straight line
steps.body: The exterior angle is 180° − 63° = 117°, which also equals 46° + 71°.

resolution.takeaway: An exterior angle equals the two remote interior angles because both calculations remove the same third angle from 180°.

beats.purpose: Name triangle types and constraints only after the relationships have been used.
beats.expectedRealization: Triangle vocabulary records properties that remain true under motion.
beats.name: Triangle constraints
beats.conciseDefinition: Every triangle's angles sum to 180°. An isosceles triangle has at least two equal sides and therefore two equal opposite angles. An exterior angle forms a linear pair with its adjacent interior angle.
beats.formalization: A + B + C = 180° · AB = AC ⇔ ∠B = ∠C · exterior = remote interior + remote interior
beats.memoryHook: Three corners make a line; equal sides face equal angles; exterior collects the far two.

beats.purpose: Chain isosceles base angles, triangle sum, and a straight-line supplement.
beats.expectedRealization: The equal-side fact controls triangle BDC, and the requested angle is outside that triangle.
beats.transitionIn: Use equal-side marks to close one triangle, then use the line through its vertex.
beats.whyNow: The learner has derived each ingredient and can now attach them to a compact contest diagram.
beats.entryBridge: Work in triangle BDC first; only afterward use straight line A–D–C.
beats.exitBridge: Triangle BDC gives 40° at D; its neighboring exterior angle is 140°.
beats.reusedRepresentation: A triangle with equal-side ticks and angle labels attached to vertices.
learnerPrompts: What does BD = DC force about angles BCD and DBC?
What is angle BDC after closing triangle BDC?
Which straight-line relationship gives angle ADB?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. The isosceles triangle gives 40° at D, and the straight line gives 140°.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Mark both base angles in triangle BDC as 70°, find its third angle, then supplement it along A–D–C.

steps.title: Transfer equality
steps.body: BD = DC, so the opposite angles DBC and BCD are both 70°.

steps.title: Use the exterior line
steps.body: Angles ADB and BDC form a straight angle, so ADB = 180° − 40° = 140°.

resolution.takeaway: Identify the triangle that owns the side equality before using the exterior supplement.

beats.purpose: Establish exhaustive, non-overlapping angle-role cases in an isosceles triangle.
beats.expectedRealization: The given 70° and x° can occupy distinct base/vertex roles, producing exactly three values.
beats.transitionIn: One isosceles diagram fixed which angles matched. Remove the labels' roles and determine every legal placement.
beats.whyNow: The learner knows the defining equality and can now reason about all possible role assignments instead of relying on one prototype.
beats.entryBridge: Separate the cases: x matches 70°, 70° is the vertex, or x is the vertex.
beats.exitBridge: The role list is exhaustive and disjoint, giving x = 70, 55, or 40 and total 165.
beats.reusedRepresentation: Equal-side ticks paired with base and vertex angle roles.
learnerPrompts: What if x and 70° are the equal base angles?
What if 70° is the vertex angle?
What if x is the vertex angle?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. The three possible values are 70, 55, and 40, whose sum is 165.
beats.incorrectFeedback: List who occupies the unique vertex role and who occupies the paired base-angle role in each case.

steps.title: Match the base angles
steps.body: If x is the other base angle with 70°, then x = 70°.

steps.title: Put 70° at the vertex
steps.body: The equal base angles share 110°, so x = 55°.

steps.title: Put x at the vertex
steps.body: The two base angles are 70° each, so x = 180° − 140° = 40°.

steps.title: Audit and add
steps.body: The unique vertex is occupied by neither named angle, by 70°, or by x; these roles cover all possibilities. Their values sum to 70 + 55 + 40 = 165.

resolution.takeaway: Completeness comes from exhausting structural roles, not merely drawing several pictures.

beats.whyNow: Return to the foundational invariant after the case analysis.
beats.entryBridge: Identify the one triangle and its three interior angles.
learnerPrompts: What remains after subtracting both known interior angles from 180°?
beats.incorrectFeedback: All three interior angles of this triangle total 180°.

resolution.takeaway: Use the angle sum inside the named triangle.

beats.purpose: Assess property-based classification in a non-prototype orientation.
beats.whyNow: Test whether rotation has been separated from defining properties.
beats.entryBridge: Read lengths and angle marks, not pose.
beats.exitBridge: Three equal sides guarantee equilateral and therefore isosceles.
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. Three equal sides make the triangle equilateral, regardless of orientation.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Ignore which direction the triangle points and use the three equal-side marks.

steps.body: Rotation preserves all side lengths. With all three sides equal, the triangle is equilateral (and also has at least two equal sides).

resolution.takeaway: Orientation never changes a length-based classification.

beats.purpose: Assess equal base angles plus angle sum.
beats.whyNow: Use the side-angle link in the reverse numerical direction from the guided problem.
beats.entryBridge: Share the remaining angle total equally between the base angles.
beats.exitBridge: The two base angles are 67° each.
learnerPrompts: How much remains after the vertex angle, and why is it split equally?
beats.incorrectFeedback: Subtract 46° from 180°, then divide the remainder between equal base angles.

steps.body: The base angles share 180° − 46° = 134°, so each is 134° ÷ 2 = 67°.

resolution.takeaway: Equal sides force an equal split of the remaining angle total.

beats.purpose: Assess exterior angle without confusing it with the adjacent interior angle.
beats.whyNow: Apply the derived relation in one step and verify it in two.
beats.entryBridge: Add the two remote interior angles, then check with the adjacent supplement.
learnerPrompts: Which two angles are remote from the exterior angle?
beats.incorrectFeedback: The exterior angle equals the sum of the two non-adjacent interior angles.

steps.body: 38° + 79° = 117°. The third interior angle is 63°, and 63° + 117° = 180° checks the result.

resolution.takeaway: Exterior is not interior; it supplements the nearby interior and collects the far two.

beats.purpose: Assess selecting the relevant triangle in a nested diagram.
beats.whyNow: Finish with a relationship that belongs to a smaller named triangle.
beats.entryBridge: Use only the three angles of triangle QRS.
beats.exitBridge: Other lines in the diagram do not enter its 180° sum.
learnerPrompts: Which three vertices name the triangle whose angle is requested?
beats.incorrectFeedback: Restrict the angle sum to triangle QRS: use its 41° and 56° angles.

resolution.takeaway: Write the triangle's name before choosing its three angles.

beats.purpose: Consolidate triangle identification, equality, and exterior checks.
beats.expectedRealization: Triangle reasoning is a sequence of property-based constraints.
beats.transitionIn: Moving vertices, rotated figures, equal sides, exterior lines, and role cases all depended on attaching facts to the correct parts.
beats.prompt: Which actions belong in a reliable triangle routine? Select all four.

options.text: Name the exact triangle being used.
Match equal sides with their opposite equal angles.
Separate an exterior angle from its adjacent interior angle.

response.feedback: Each action keeps a constraint attached to the right object.

beats.correctFeedback: Yes. Name the triangle, use its total, transfer equality, and distinguish exterior from interior.
beats.incorrectFeedback: All four prevent a common angle-chasing mix-up.

steps.body: A diagram may contain several triangles and lines. Label the active triangle first, then apply only the constraints owned by its sides and angles.

resolution.takeaway: Properties, not appearance, determine a triangle's consequences.

beats.purpose: Create the successor need for the Pythagorean relationship.
beats.expectedRealization: Fixing one angle at 90° strongly constrains both remaining angles and side lengths.
beats.transitionIn: Equal sides added one constraint to a triangle. A fixed right angle adds a different one.
beats.prompt: If one angle is locked at 90°, what can the other two angles do, and what new relationship might connect the three side lengths?
beats.takeaway: A right triangle has only 90° left for its acute angles—and its side lengths hide another invariant.

notes: Design: G1's straight-angle benchmark becomes a triangle angle-sum invariant. Equal-side marks add a second constraint independent of orientation, and exterior angles are derived from triangle sum plus a linear pair. The first authentic problem chains those facts; the second proves case completeness through the unique vertex/base roles.

Beat outline: moving-vertex puzzle -> equal-side lock -> rotated classification -> exterior derivation -> name constraints -> guided authentic chase -> authentic role cases -> five independent problems -> consolidation -> right-triangle hook.

Both mapped animations are referenced unchanged and appear after submission. The first uses its whole timeline; the role-case scene uses its three readable case states, while the declarative resolution performs the final completeness audit and sum. Existing generic visuals suffice; no renderer or animation source changes were made.
Generated answers were recomputed by angle sums and equal-angle splits, with independent supplement, exterior-angle, classification, or option audits. The lesson remains draft pending human review.
